ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: Suppose the money supply in an economy doubles permanently while real output, velocity, and everything else stay the same. Which statement best explains the long-run effect?

options.text: The price level roughly doubles, because the same real output is exchanged for twice as much money.
options.why: With MV = PQ and V and Q unchanged, a doubling of M doubles P.

options.text: The interest rate falls permanently, because the supply of money is larger.
options.why: In the long run the real interest rate is set by saving and investment, not the money supply.

options.text: Real output doubles, because people have twice as much money to spend.
options.why: In the long run real output is set by resources and technology, not by money.

options.text: Velocity doubles, because people hold less money relative to their income.
options.why: The scenario holds velocity constant.

options.text: The price level is unchanged, because real output is unchanged.
options.why: With output and velocity fixed, a larger money supply must raise the price level.

facts: variant=Suppose the money supply in an economy d

ap_macroeconomics-m02.stem: Workers and firms correctly expect 5 percent inflation, and actual inflation turns out to be 5 percent. Which statement best explains why this anticipated inflation has smaller real effects than unexpected inflation?

options.text: Wages and contracts already include the expected inflation, so real wages and relative prices are not distorted.
options.why: When inflation is anticipated, nominal contracts adjust in advance, leaving real values nearly unchanged.

options.text: Anticipated inflation eliminates menu costs and shoe-leather costs completely.
options.why: Some costs of inflation remain even when it is expected.

options.text: Anticipated inflation raises real output permanently, because firms expect higher prices.
options.why: Anticipated inflation does not raise real output.

options.text: Anticipated inflation redistributes income from borrowers to lenders.
options.why: That redistribution is caused by unexpected inflation.

options.text: Anticipated inflation lowers the real value of all contracts, because prices rise faster than wages.
options.why: Contracts that include expected inflation keep their real value.

facts: variant=Workers and firms correctly expect 5 per

ap_macroeconomics-m03.stem: A government runs large budget deficits for many years and its national debt rises steadily. Which statement best explains how the higher debt can affect future budgets?

options.text: Interest payments on the larger debt become a bigger part of spending, which can force higher taxes or less spending on other programs.
options.why: Debt service is a claim on future budgets, which raises future tax needs or reduces other spending.

options.text: The debt has no effect on future budgets, because the government owes the debt to itself.
options.why: Part of the debt is held by the public and by foreigners, which requires interest payments.

options.text: Interest payments fall as debt rises, because the government can borrow at lower rates.
options.why: A larger debt does not lower interest payments.

options.text: The debt automatically lowers the inflation rate, because the government spends less.
options.why: Deficits and debt do not automatically lower inflation.

options.text: The debt raises future budgets' surpluses, because borrowed funds increase tax revenue directly.
options.why: Borrowing does not raise tax revenue by itself.

facts: variant=A government runs large budget deficits

ap_macroeconomics-m04.stem: A government wants to raise the long-run growth rate of real GDP without raising the inflation rate. Which of the following policies is most consistent with that goal, and why?

options.text: Subsidizing research and worker training, because this raises productivity and shifts long-run aggregate supply right without adding to demand.
options.why: Supply-side measures raise potential output, which lowers price pressure while raising growth.

options.text: Cutting interest rates to the lowest level possible, because cheaper credit always raises productivity.
options.why: Lower rates stimulate demand in the short run but do not raise potential output.

options.text: Increasing the money supply rapidly, because more money raises real GDP in the long run.
options.why: Rapid money growth raises prices, not long-run output.

options.text: Imposing price controls on all goods, because lower prices raise real GDP.
options.why: Price controls distort markets and do not raise potential output.

options.text: Raising government purchases permanently, because spending raises potential output directly.
options.why: Higher purchases raise demand and can add to inflation.

facts: variant=A government wants to raise the long-run
